Van Allen Belts:

Inner belt much more radiation and shorter distance inner-edge to outer-edge (1,000 km - 9,600 km at its thickest point)

Outer belt: much lower radiation and larger distance inner-edge to outer-edge (13,500 km - 58,000 at its thickest point km)

Apollo flight trajectories did not fly through the stronger (radiation) inner belt but even if they had, at escape velocity would have only spent 12.9 minutes inside the area.

Apollo flight trajectories did fly through the weaker (radiation) outer belts, and flew through their thinnest span. Even if they flew through the thickest band of the outer belts, traveling at 40,000 km/h, the crew would have been in that area for only a little over an hour.

Total radiation exposure for the crew for the entire mission (including outgoing + incoming transits of the Van Allen belts) was dependent on the mission flown but varied between 0.16 and 1.14 rads.

Given that 25 rads is the lowest dose to cause observable blood changes, the absorbed radiation from the belts did not pose any short-term (acute) risks to the astronauts. Most of their absorbed radiation came from high-energy particles outside the Van Allen belts and Earth's magnetic shielding.

TL;DR: Mission planning isn't part of "Rocket Science" because it's easy, and minimizing radiation exposure was definitely part of the mission planning.

Answer to #9: Everyone needs to read up on the radio systemS (PLURAL) employed by the Apollo Command / Service module (CSM). It's not just for voice traffic. All of the systems reported back telemetry so that the flight controllers can calculate positions, fuel levels, roll rates, etc., without needing to ask the crew "What does gauge X say?"

When the CSM and the Lunar Lander (LM) are separated (as they are during the LM's descent to the lunar surface), Mission Control has multiple ways to talk to the units. Mission control can talk thru the CSM to the LM or talk directly with the LM and in fact was doing both at the same time (although the CSM was in a stable orbit and less attention was paid to its systems) than the critical readouts of the LM during lunar landing.

During Apollo 11's (first manned) landing, Mission Control Center (MCC) had issues with direct communication (and thus telemetry feedback) after the LM came around the back side of the moon and was approaching its landing path.

MCC had a strict go / no-go rule hierarchy to guide whether they could proceed with lowering their altitude and going for landing. There were several times In fact, when Gene Kranz (flight director) was close to calling an abort on Apollo 11's landing as MCC lost and regained telemetry feeds with the LM. The flight rules were strict: MCC would not proceed without knowing the fuel-level, attitude, roll-rate, system configuration, etc. of the craft before taking action [312], [313], [314] (etc.) in the flight plan... etc. The reason is straight-forward: If you fail, you need to know why and you can't know why without knowing the current configuration, altitude, position, roll rate, etc., of the space craft at that point in time.

The whole point of this is there are multiple radio feeds, multiple antennas and multiple people watching and interacting with both space craft at this time.

And the simple answer regarding the LM ascent footage is that lots of simulation-practice and an earth-based remote-control of the lunar camera gimble allowed the footage to be captured and then transmitted back to Earth. Ed Fendall was the remote-controller of the camera gimble

And since this is a radio broadcast (and recorded on Earth) you don't have to worry about film anything -- there was no film on that camera, same as the live shot of Neil's descent down the LM lander.
